subtitle: Questions that need a row to look at its neighbors.

eyebrow: A small time series — sort first!
caption: Every operation in this lesson depends on row order — sort by date before you start.

code:
daily["ma3"] = daily["sales"].rolling(3).mean()

# row 0,1: NaN (no full window yet)
# row 2: (120+135+110)/3 = 121.67
caption: rolling(3) builds a window of the current row plus the two before it, then you aggregate it.

code:
daily["sales"].rolling(3, min_periods=1).mean()  # partial start
daily["sales"].rolling(3, center=True).mean()    # window around the row
daily["sales"].rolling("3D").mean()               # time-span window
caption: center=True smooths a chart nicely but leaks future info if used as a model feature.
cummax, cummin, cumprod work the same way. expanding's window grows by one row each step.

code:
daily["prev"] = daily["sales"].shift(1)     # pandas LAG()
daily["change"] = daily["sales"].diff()
daily["pct"] = daily["sales"].pct_change()
# day 2: +12.5% / day 6: -40%
caption: shift(-1) looks forward, like LEAD(). The first row is always NaN — there's no previous value.

code:
o = orders.sort_values(["customer_id", "order_date"]).copy()
g = o.groupby("customer_id")
o["cust_running"] = g["amount"].cumsum()
o["prev_amount"] = g["amount"].shift(1)
o["order_no"] = g.cumcount() + 1
o["days_since_prev"] = g["order_date"].diff().dt.days
caption: The calculation restarts for each group — order_no is pandas' ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY ...).
